name: Device Monitoring
title: Device Monitoring
answer: Device monitoring is the practice of paying companies to scan what students do on school devices and accounts for signs of self harm, violence, or other risks. It matters because the evidence does not support vendors' claims that these tools save lives, and monitoring raises real questions of trust and fairness, especially for marginalized students. Districts that use it should require trained human review of every alert and publish a clear policy about what is monitored and what happens to alerts.

sections.body: Device monitoring means districts pay outside companies to watch what students do on school devices and accounts, scanning searches, messages, and documents for signs of self harm, violence, or other risks. Vendors often say these tools save lives, but the book states the evidence does not support those claims. The problem is not only whether the signals mean anything, but whether acting on them actually prevents harm. Monitoring also raises questions of trust and fairness, because flagged private searches or messages can expose or discipline students in ways that damage trust. The idea therefore solves a perceived need for early warning while creating new risks that districts must weigh carefully.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, monitoring runs in the background on school devices and accounts, with tools scanning searches, messages, and documents and flagging possible risks. The book does not give grade band examples, so the practice is described at the district level. A district that chooses monitoring should set strict conditions, starting with a trained person reviewing every alert before any action is taken. The district should also publish a clear policy explaining what is monitored, when it is monitored, and what happens to alerts. Monitoring outside school hours, and any direct contact with police by a vendor, deserve especially hard questions.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels the evidence as not supporting vendor claims. A review found no evidence that social media surveillance by schools improves student health or safety, and noted it may harm marginalized young people (Burke et al., 2020). A review of 31 studies found surveillance technology is concentrated in schools serving poor and minoritized students, with mixed effects on how safe students feel (Sheikh et al., 2024). A study using monitoring data from 2,600 schools found online risk signals were associated with later severe self harm alerts (Sumner et al., 2021), which shows the signals mean something but does not show monitoring prevents harm. A survey found young adults saw less benefit and more risk in school surveillance than parents, teachers, or administrators, and that nonheterosexual and minority respondents saw the highest risk (Burke et al., 2023). The study of 14 monitoring companies found round the clock monitoring outside school, AI flagging with limited human review, and some companies contacting police on their own (O'Daffer et al., 2025).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The book sets clear limits and risks. Monitoring can damage trust when students are flagged for private searches or messages and then exposed or disciplined. It can also fall unfairly on marginalized students, and young adults, especially nonheterosexual and minority respondents, see the highest risk. The decisions that stay with a person include reviewing every alert through a trained human before any action is taken. The district must publish a clear policy on what is monitored, when, and what happens to alerts. Monitoring outside school hours and any direct contact with police by a vendor deserve especially hard questions.
